fields.Front: What is the core difference between a pointer and a reference in C++?
fields.Back: A reference must be bound at declaration, can never be null, and can never be rebound to alias a different object. A pointer can be reassigned, can be null, and requires explicit dereferencing (*p) to access the pointee.

fields.Front: What does RAII stand for, and what problem does it solve in C++?
fields.Back: Resource Acquisition Is Initialization — a resource (memory, file handle, lock) is acquired in a constructor and released in the destructor, so it's automatically freed when the owning object goes out of scope, even if an exception unwinds the stack.

fields.Front: How do you write a minimal RAII wrapper around a raw FILE* handle in C++?
fields.Back:
class FileGuard {
    FILE* fp;
public:
    explicit FileGuard(const char* path) : fp(fopen(path, "r")) {}
    ~FileGuard() { if (fp) fclose(fp); }
    FILE* get() const { return fp; }
};

fields.Front: What's the key ownership difference between std::unique_ptr and std::shared_ptr?
fields.Back: unique_ptr has sole, non-copyable ownership (move-only), with near-zero overhead over a raw pointer. shared_ptr uses atomic reference counting so multiple owners can share the object, which is freed only when the last shared_ptr is destroyed.

fields.Front: How do you create a std::unique_ptr<Widget> and move ownership into a function taking it by value?
fields.Back:
auto w = std::make_unique<Widget>(args);
takeOwnership(std::move(w));
// w is now null; caller must not use it

fields.Front: What memory-leak risk does std::weak_ptr solve when two objects hold std::shared_ptrs to each other?
fields.Back: A reference cycle between two shared_ptrs means their counts never reach zero, leaking both objects. weak_ptr holds a non-owning reference that doesn't affect the count; call .lock() to get a temporary shared_ptr only if the object is still alive.

fields.Front: What is an rvalue reference (T&&) used for in C++?
fields.Back: It binds to temporaries/movable values so a function overload can detect 'this object is about to be destroyed anyway' and steal (move) its internal resources instead of deep-copying them.

fields.Front: How do you implement a move constructor for a class that owns a raw heap buffer data and size len?
fields.Back:
MyBuf(MyBuf&& other) noexcept
    : data(other.data), len(other.len) {
    other.data = nullptr;
    other.len = 0;
}

fields.Front: What is the Rule of Zero in C++?
fields.Back: Prefer composing a class entirely from members that already manage their own resources (smart pointers, containers, strings) so you never write any of the five special member functions — the compiler-generated versions are already correct.

fields.Front: Why does declaring a custom destructor implicitly disable the compiler-generated move constructor in C++?
fields.Back: A user-declared destructor signals custom resource-management logic, so the compiler won't risk synthesizing a possibly-unsafe move constructor. Moves then silently fall back to copies unless you define the move constructor yourself (or explicitly = default it).

fields.Front: What does const on a C++ member function guarantee?
fields.Back: It promises not to modify any non-mutable member of the object — the implicit this becomes a pointer-to-const — which is what allows the function to be called on const instances and const references.

fields.Front: Between const int* p and int* const p, which one is a pointer that cannot itself be reassigned (but may modify the pointed-to int)?
fields.Back: int* const p — the const binds to p itself. const int* p is the opposite: a reassignable pointer to a constant int.

fields.Front: How do you declare a C++ function template that returns the larger of two values of any comparable type?
fields.Back:
template <typename T>
T max_of(const T& a, const T& b) {
    return (a > b) ? a : b;
}

fields.Front: What is a vtable in C++, and when does a class get one?
fields.Back: A per-class array of function pointers used to resolve virtual calls at runtime. A class gets a vtable (and each instance a hidden vptr) as soon as it declares or inherits at least one virtual function.

fields.Front: Why should a base class's destructor be virtual if you plan to delete a derived object through a base class pointer?
fields.Back: Without a virtual destructor, delete basePtr only invokes the base class's destructor and skips the derived class's cleanup — undefined behavior, typically a resource leak.

fields.Front: What's the core tradeoff between stack and heap allocation in C++?
fields.Back: Stack: fixed size, automatic lifetime tied to scope, very fast (just a pointer bump), but limited (~MB). Heap: manually managed via new/delete or smart pointers, flexible size, slower due to allocator bookkeeping, lifetime independent of scope.

fields.Front: Give an example of undefined behavior in C++ that the compiler is not required to diagnose.
fields.Back: Dereferencing a null or dangling pointer, signed integer overflow, or reading an uninitialized variable — the standard places no requirement on the outcome, so the compiler may optimize as if it never happens, sometimes with surprising results.

fields.Front: How do you iterate a std::vector<int> and erase all even elements using the erase-remove idiom?
fields.Back:
v.erase(
    std::remove_if(v.begin(), v.end(),
        [](int x) { return x % 2 == 0; }),
    v.end());

fields.Front: What STL container gives O(log n) sorted insertion/lookup, and which alternative gives O(1)-average lookup with no ordering guarantee?
fields.Back: std::map/std::set (red-black tree, O(log n), kept sorted). std::unordered_map/std::unordered_set give O(1) average via hashing but no ordering guarantee.

fields.Text: The Rule of Five says a class that manages a resource manually should typically define all of: {{c1::destructor}}, {{c2::copy constructor}}, {{c3::copy assignment operator}}, {{c4::move constructor}}, and {{c5::move assignment operator}}.
